description_full: Weibo Corporation, through its subsidiaries, operates as a social media platform for people to create, discover, and distribute content in the People's Republic of China. It operates through two segments, Advertising and Marketing Services; and Value-Added Services. The company offers discovery products to help users discover content on its platform; self-expression products that enable its users to express themselves on its platform; and social products to promote social interaction between users on its platform. It also provides advertising and marketing solutions, such as social display advertisements; and promoted marketing offerings, such as Fans Headline, Weibo Express, and promoted feeds, as well as promoted trends and search products that appear alongside user's trends discovery and search behaviors. In addition, the company offers products, such as trends, search, video/live streaming, and editing tools; content customization, copyright contents pooling, and user interaction development; and search list recommendation, trends list recommendation, and Weibo app opening advertisements. Further, it provides back-end management, traffic support, and product services for better displaying and promotion of its account and content; an open application platform that allows users to log into third-party applications with their Weibo account for sharing third-party content on its platform; and Weibo Wallet, a product that enables platform partners to conduct interest generation activities on Weibo, such as handing out red envelops and coupons. It serves ordinary people, celebrities, opinion leaders, and other public figures or influencers, as well as media outlets, businesses, government agencies, charities, and other organizations. The company was formerly known as T.CN Corporation and changed its name to Weibo Corporation in 2012. The company was founded in 2009 and is based in Beijing, the People's Republic of China.

financial_summary: Weibo Corporation is a small-cap communication services business with a $1.5B market cap on $1.8B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at -1% over the past three years and +14% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding. Operating margins are expanding by +3.0pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 114% against a 7% cost of capital — a 107-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $477M in free cash flow — roughly 27 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.16× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage runs at 5.6×.
Management returns a meaningful 12.9% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 8.2% of the shares.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (1.7) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Very elevated short interest (20.0% of float) — sophisticated money is betting against the business
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Advertising-cycle exposure and content/regulatory risk — a single platform policy shift or ad-spend contraction cascades through the P&L quickly.
Cord-cutting acceleration and audience fragmentation — legacy distribution bundles unravel faster than subscription revenue can replace them.
AI-generated content commoditisation — as creation costs collapse toward zero, content libraries lose pricing power and differentiation narrows.

Trading at a 78% margin of safety to estimated fair value — a real cushion against errors in the estimate
Trading near the bottom of its 52-week range — the market is offering a discount
Valued at a 84% discount to sector median EV/EBITDA
ROIC sits in the top quartile of Communication Services peers — the moat is wider than the neighbourhood
Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk

sect: Its 26% operating margin runs 18pp above the Communication Services median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.29x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-14.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.06 across 171 companies in the universe; the top four hold 36% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 32% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 45% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 26% and a beta of 0.82, it moves roughly with the market.
About $5.8M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 42% in the 2020 crash and 69% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 78% below its DCF fair value of $27.76, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 34%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $21.16 to $38.30 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Communication Services peers: P/E 5.1 vs 15.4, EV/EBITDA 1.5 vs 9.9 and P/FCF 3.2 vs 11.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 70% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 31.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 60.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 16 covering analysts target $7.93 on average, 29% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 114% clears the cost of capital of 7.0% by 107pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.97).
It converts 27% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.16x.
ROE of 11% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.8x equity multiplier).
It spends 18.5% of revenue on R&D and 2.4% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $308.9M (20% of market cap).
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.69 in the distress zone.
Its debt comes due soon (maturity wall about 0.5 years out), so refinancing terms matter.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -1.5% over 3 years, 0.8% over 5 years and 13.9% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 28%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -7.6% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (2.4% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders own 8.2%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 24%.
It returns 12.9% a year to shareholders (9.9% in dividends).
The share count has grown 1.5% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
Short interest is elevated at 20.0% of the float, 17.9 days to cover.
people: With about 5,651 employees, each generates about $311K of revenue, 0.5x the Communication Services median, and revenue has grown 16.3% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $84K of free cash flow per employee.
